displayQuote: It Is Better to Know Nothing than to Know What Ain't So

meta.title: Who really said "It Is Better to Know Nothing than to Know What Ain't So"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Artemus Ward. Josh Billings printed it in dialect in 1869 and collected it in Everybody's Friend (1874). Ward died in 1867, two years earlier.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It Is Better to Know Nothing than to Know What Ain't So'?
meta.ogDescription: Josh Billings wrote it in dialect — "better tew know nothing than two know what ain't so" (1874). Artemus Ward only got the credit from 1897.

answer.label: Not Artemus Ward — actually Josh Billings
answer.authorDates: 1818–1885 · American humorist who wrote in comic phonetic dialect
answer.sourceLine: The line is Josh Billings’s, and it survives in his own trademark misspelling, as the 1874 book prints it: “I honestly beleave it iz better tew know nothing than two know what ain’t so.” A slightly different dialect wording ran in newspapers under his byline from May 1869, before the sentence was collected in Everybody’s Friend (1874), in a section of aphorisms headed “Sollum Thoughts.” Artemus Ward died in 1867, two years before the earliest printing anyone has documented; his name was attached to the saying not until 1897, on the record Quote Investigator assembled.

source.heading: The 1874 book — and the newspaper columns five years before it

docMeta.dd: Everybody’s Friend, or Josh Billing’s Encyclopedia and Proverbial Philosophy of Wit and Humor
1874 · American Publishing Company, Hartford, Connecticut · illustrated by Thomas Nast and others
“Sollum Thoughts” by Josh Billings, Harrisburg Telegraph, 7 May 1869 — the earliest instance Quote Investigator documents

source.excerpt:
Hope iz a hen that lays more eggs than she kan hatch out.
Better leave yure child virtew than money; but this iz a sekret known only tew a few.
I honestly beleave it iz better tew know nothing than two know what ain’t so.
About the hardest work a phellow kan do iz tew spark two galls at once, and preserve a good average.
trail: May 1869 — The saying runs in newspapers under Josh Billings’s byline, in a column of “Sollum Thoughts.” Quote Investigator documents printings in the Harrisburg Telegraph of 7 May 1869 and The Border Sentinel of 21 May 1869 ↗.
1874 — It is collected in Everybody’s Friend, under “Affurisms: Sollum Thoughts.” You can read the sentence in the original dialect in the Library of Congress copy scanned at the Internet Archive ↗.

1897 — Thirty years after Artemus Ward’s death, a rephrased version is credited to him in The North-Western Journal of Education — with his name misspelled “Artemas.” Quote Investigator records the citation ↗.

The irony — a rephrased form of the aphorism does appear in The Complete Works of Artemus Ward, exactly once: “You’d better not know so much, than know so many things that ain’t so,” in Melville D. Landon’s biographical sketch, where it is credited to Josh Billings. Search the Project Gutenberg text for that wording ↗ — Ward never wrote it.
source.excerptNote: The spelling is Billings’s own, not a transcription error — the whole book is written that way, and “two” here is his rendering of “tew.” The smooth modern form everyone quotes (“It is better to know nothing than to know what ain’t so”) is a standard-spelling modernisation of this sentence, not a separate line by a separate author.

source.rightsNote: Everybody’s Friend was published in Hartford by the American Publishing Company in 1874, and the sentence was already in American newspapers in 1869 — far earlier than the 1931 US copyright threshold — so the text is in the public domain in the United States. Josh Billings died in 1885. The full 1874 volume is freely readable at the Internet Archive, and The Complete Works of Artemus Ward is free at Project Gutenberg.

author.name: Josh Billings
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: Josh Billings, the deliberate misspeller
author.bio: Josh Billings was the pen name of Henry Wheeler Shaw (born 21 April 1818, Lanesborough, Massachusetts; died 14 October 1885, Monterey, California), one of the most widely read American humorists of the post–Civil War decades. His signature device was eccentric phonetic spelling — “iz” for is, “tew” for to, “beleave” for believe — wrapped around aphorisms sharp enough to survive the joke. That spelling is exactly why his best lines kept getting handed to other people: for most of the last century and a half, a reader searching for “it is better to know nothing” had no way to reach “it iz better tew know nothing,” so the sentence circulated unmoored from its author — long enough for four other humorists to be given the credit before quotation databases started indexing both spellings.

misattribution.heading: Four famous names, one actual author
misattribution.intro: This sentence belongs to a whole family of American wisecracks about confident ignorance, and the family has been passed round the great humorists like a hat. Quote Investigator traces the specific wording here to Josh Billings and then watches the credit migrate, decade by decade, to bigger names.

items.why: Charles Farrar Browne — “Artemus Ward” — died of consumption at Southampton on 6 March 1867 ↗, two years before the saying’s earliest documented printing. Quote Investigator finds the first Ward ascription in 1897 ↗, in The North-Western Journal of Education, which even misspells him “Artemas.” Wikiquote’s Artemus Ward page does not carry the line at all ↗.

A rephrased version was assigned to Twain by a religious orator in The Pacific Unitarian in 1899, fourteen years after Billings’s death. Scholars at the Center for Mark Twain Studies find no substantive evidence for the Twain versions of this family ↗.
In 1900 The Land of Sunshine printed a variant as a Lincoln remark ↗ — “It’s better not to know quite so many things than to know so many things that ain’t so.”
A loosened variant is routinely hung on Rogers; Quote Investigator cites a 1978 New York Magazine instance ↗. WIST notes the Rogers, Twain and Ward credits all trace back to Billings ↗.

items.who: Nobody — but it has been tidied up
items.why: The familiar smooth sentence is a standard-spelling rendering of Billings’s dialect original. Wikiquote records the 1874 dialect text under “Sollum Thoughts” ↗; the modernised form is a translation of it, not a rival quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: One author, one book, one section: Josh Billings, Everybody’s Friend (1874), “Affurisms: Sollum Thoughts” — with the line already in print under his byline in May 1869. Quote Investigator recommends the 1874 version because it appeared in a book under Billings’s own imprimatur ↗.

context.heading: Why this one keeps changing hands
lead: Bad spelling is a terrible way to protect your copyright. Billings built a career on writing “iz” and “tew” and “beleave” — it was the joke, the brand, the reason people bought the book. But it means that for a century and a half, every reader who wanted to quote him has had to smooth him out first, and a smoothed-out sentence carries no fingerprints. For most of that stretch, a search for “it is better to know nothing” led nowhere near Billings; only recently have citation-first databases such as WIST and Wikiquote begun printing the dialect original and the standard-spelling rendering side by side.

So the line went looking for a father, and nineteenth-century America had a surplus of candidates. Artemus Ward got it in 1897, Mark Twain in 1899, Abraham Lincoln in 1900, Will Rogers much later. Quote Investigator describes the mechanism plainly: sayings in this family get rephrased, hybridised with each other, and re-ascribed from one prominent humorist to the next — which is how a line first printed in a Pennsylvania newspaper in 1869 ends up on a poster with somebody else’s face on it.
detailsBody: The cousin everyone confuses it with. “It ain’t what you don’t know that gets you into trouble — it’s what you know for sure that just ain’t so” is a different saying, usually pinned on Mark Twain and used to open the film The Big Short. Quote Investigator concludes its creator is anonymous, while treating the genuine 1874 Billings line as the seed the family grew from ↗.

An older cousin, and a foreign one. Quote Investigator notes a thematic precursor in a 1747 history of Persia — “it is better to know nothing, than to apprehend we know what we know not” — and a separate branch in Nietzsche’s Also Sprach Zarathustra, rendered in Thomas Common’s 1911 English as “Better know nothing than half-know many things!” ↗. Neither is the sentence on this page.
context.pull: A joke about confident wrong knowledge became a case study in confident wrong knowledge.

sourcesVerified.claim: Josh Billings originated the saying; it appeared in the Harrisburg Telegraph on 7 May 1869 and in Everybody's Friend (1874) as "I honestly beleave it iz better tew know nothing than two know what ain't so"; by 1897 The North-Western Journal of Education reassigned it to Artemus Ward (misspelled "Artemas"); later reassignments include Mark Twain (1899), Abraham Lincoln (1900) and Will Rogers (1978); a 1747 history of Persia is a thematic precursor.

The Library of Congress copy of Everybody's Friend (Hartford: American Publishing Company, 1874) is scanned in full, and its "Affurisms: Sollum Thoughts" section contains "I honestly beleave it iz better tew know nothing than two know what ain't so" alongside "Hope iz a hen that lays more eggs than she kan hatch out" and "Better leave yure child virtew than money."

In The Complete Works of Artemus Ward the aphorism occurs exactly once — in Melville D. Landon's prefatory biographical sketch, quoted as Josh Billings's ("You'd better not know so much, than know so many things that ain't so") — and nowhere in Ward's own writings; the sketch gives Charles Farrar Browne's dates as born 26 April 1834 and died 6 March 1867 at Southampton.
Wikiquote records "I honestly beleave it iz better tew know nothing than two know what ain't so" under Everybody's Friend (1874), "Sollum Thoughts," with a standard-spelling rendering noted.
Wikiquote's Artemus Ward page does not list this saying, or the "know so many things that ain't so" variant, in any section including Misattributed or Disputed.

Henry Wheeler Shaw (Josh Billings) was born 21 April 1818 in Lanesborough, Massachusetts and died 14 October 1885 in Monterey, California; he was an American humorist and lecturer who wrote with eccentric phonetic spelling, and Everybody's Friend is among his books.
Charles Farrar Browne, who wrote as Artemus Ward, was born 26 April 1834 and died 6 March 1867.

WIST records the quotation under Josh Billings with the citation Everybody's Friend, "Sollum Thoughts" (1874), and notes that variant forms have been wrongly credited to Will Rogers, Mark Twain and Artemus Ward.

Quote Investigator states that scholars at the Center for Mark Twain Studies found no substantive evidence for the Twain ascription in this family of sayings, that Ward, Billings, Kin Hubbard and Will Rogers all receive credit for members of it, and that the genuine 1874 Billings item acted as a seed for the family.
Nietzsche's Also Sprach Zarathustra contains "Lieber Nichts wissen, als Vieles halb wissen!", rendered in Thomas Common's 1911 translation as "Better know nothing than half-know many things!"
